p4_b0.ocr: In the study by Jousset et al., 2004, the objective was to compare RTW in patients participating in a multidisciplinary functional restoration programme to those in active individual therapy, revealing a significantly lower mean number of self-reported sick-leave days, with outcome measures including sick-leave days over two years, RTW within one week, and subjective ratings of ability to work and improved physical condition.

p4_b3.ocr: Joy et al., 2001 focused on RTW after a work-hardening programme, measuring part-time or full-time RTW status at follow-up, alongside functional capacity, age, injury length (days), program duration (days), work status, pain level, pain tolerance (% improvement), and activity tolerance (% improvement). Lambeek et al., 2010 evaluated an integrated care programme for chronic low back pain, assessing sick leave duration until full RTW, with outcomes on time off work, pain intensity, and functional status. Schene et al., 2007 found significant differences between TAU and TAU + OT regarding RTW timing and total hours worked, measuring depression, work resumption, work stress, service use, and economic evaluation.

p4_b4.ocr: Sullivan et al., 2006 compared RTW percentages among PGAP + PT versus PT alone, focusing on full-time employment status and various psychological factors. Vanderploeg et al., 2008 examined RTW or school return in two rehabilitation approaches, assessing employment status, life satisfaction, social aspects, and emotional well-being.
